title: Hannah asks, and gives back
sum: Elkanah of Ramah has two wives: Peninnah, who has children, and Hannah, whom he loves but who has none. Every year at the feast in Shiloh, Peninnah taunts Hannah until she weeps and will not eat (1:1–8). One year Hannah goes to the sanctuary and prays silently, vowing that if the LORD gives her a son, she will give him back for life. Eli the priest, watching her lips move, takes her for a drunk, then blesses her when she explains (1:9–18).

The LORD remembers Hannah, and she bears a son and names him Samuel, saying she asked the LORD for him. When he is weaned she brings him to Shiloh with a sacrifice and hands him over to the LORD, as she promised (1:19–28). The story of Israel's kingdom begins with a barren woman's prayer.
readings: Read as a story of prayer

Hannah prays with her heart, not her voice, and her prayer is misunderstood by the priest. Jewish teachers took her as the model of prayer: speak from the heart, move the lips, keep the voice low. The chapter shows God answering not the powerful priest but the woman in tears.
Read as the start of a nation's story

The book could have begun with a king. It begins instead with a family at a feast and a woman without a child. The pattern of the barren mother (Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Samson's mother) signals that God is about to do something new for all Israel through this one child.

views.H: Traditional readers take the family and the yearly feast at Shiloh as real events of about 1100 BC, with the tabernacle then standing at Shiloh (Joshua 18:1). Elkanah's family tree in 1 Chronicles 6 makes him a Levite living in Ephraim, which explains how his son could serve at the sanctuary.
views.C: Many critics note that the naming explanation, "I asked the LORD for him" (sha'al), fits the name Saul (Sha'ul) better than Samuel, and suggest the birth story was first told of Saul. Others answer that the wordplay is loose, as Hebrew name stories often are, and that the book deliberately points ahead to Saul.
views.L: The chapter is built on asking and giving: Hannah asks, God gives, and Hannah gives back what was asked. Literary readers note how the narrator lets the characters' words carry the feeling: Elkanah's kind but clumsy question, Eli's mistake, and Hannah's quiet answers.
views.J: The Talmud draws many rules of prayer from Hannah (Bavli Berakhot 31a–b): pray with focus, form the words with the lips, and do not raise the voice. This chapter and Hannah's song are read in synagogues on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, because tradition says Hannah was remembered on that day.
views.X: Christians have read Hannah alongside Elizabeth and Mary: women whose children were gifts of God and given back to him. Luke's account of Jesus' birth and childhood echoes the Samuel story closely (Luke 1–2).

deep.b: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Samson's mother and Hannah all wait for children, and each child becomes a turning point. In each story God is shown to be the one who opens the womb, and the child's life is from the start a gift. Hannah's story is the last in the Hebrew Bible, and the most inward: we hear her prayer, her vow and her song. In Luke, Elizabeth is the last of the line, and Mary's son comes with no human father at all.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two kinds of asking
deep.b: My own reading: the Hebrew root sha'al, "ask," runs through chapter 1 (1:17, 1:20, 1:27, 1:28) and then returns in chapter 8, when the people "ask" Samuel for a king (8:10), and in Saul's name, "the one asked for." I suggest the book means the two askings to be read together. Hannah asks God for a child and gives him back; Israel asks for a king to be like the nations and does not intend to give anything back. The same verb measures faith and its opposite. Scholars have long noted the Saul wordplay; reading it as a deliberate contrast between two kinds of asking is my own suggestion.

echoes: Genesis 16:1–2; Genesis 21:1–2; Genesis 30:1–2; Genesis 30:22–24; Judges 13:2–5; Numbers 6:1–21; Numbers 30:6–15; Luke 1:5–25; Luke 2:22–24

settings.to: the LORD of Armies, prayed silently at the sanctuary in Shiloh
settings.when: at the yearly feast, after years without a child and her rival's taunts
settings.why: Hannah asks for a son and promises to give him back to the LORD for life. No razor will touch his head, like a lifelong Nazirite (compare Numbers 6:1–21 and Judges 13:5). The vow turns her private grief into a gift for all Israel: the son she asks for will become the prophet who anoints Israel's first kings. Her silent prayer, which Eli mistakes for drunkenness, became the rabbis' model of how to pray (Bavli Berakhot 31a).

settings.to: Eli the priest, at the LORD's house in Shiloh
settings.when: when she brings the weaned boy with a sacrifice
settings.why: Hannah reminds Eli that she is the woman he once took for drunk, and that her prayer was answered. Her words play on the verb "ask" (Hebrew sha'al), which sounds like the name Saul. Many readers hear a hint already that the one Israel "asked for" will be a king named Saul, while the child given back to God is Samuel.

traditions.q: Should children be baptized, or dedicated to God as Hannah gave Samuel to the LORD?
views: Infants should be baptized soon after birth, because baptism frees them from original sin and gives a grace no one can earn (Catechism 1250–1252).
Infants are baptized, anointed with chrism and given Communion in the same service, so they are full members of the Church from the start.
Infants should be baptized, since God's promise is for them and faith is God's gift, not a human work (Augsburg Confession 9; Luther, Large Catechism).
Children of believers should be baptized, as Israel's sons were circumcised, because they belong to the covenant (Westminster Confession 28.4; Colossians 2:11–12).

Baptism is for those who confess faith in Christ, and is done by immersion (Baptist Faith and Message, article 7; London Confession 29). Many Baptist churches hold a service to dedicate infants instead, often pointing to Hannah.
Baptism belongs only to those who have repented and believe (Schleitheim Confession, article 1). This conviction gave the Anabaptists their name, re-baptizers, and many died for it.

title: Hannah's song and Eli's sons
sum: Hannah sings a song of praise: the LORD breaks the strong and lifts the weak, gives children to the barren, brings low and raises up, and will give strength to his king (2:1–10). The family goes home, and Samuel stays to serve the LORD under Eli (2:11).

Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are worthless men. They take meat from the sacrifices by force and treat the LORD's offering with contempt (2:12–17). Meanwhile young Samuel grows in favor, and Hannah has five more children (2:18–21, 2:26). Eli rebukes his sons weakly (2:22–25). A man of God comes to Eli with a terrible word: his family will lose the priesthood, his sons will die on one day, and God will raise up a faithful priest (2:27–36).
readings: Read as a song of reversals

Hannah's song turns the world upside down: the strong fall, the hungry eat, the poor sit with princes. The chapter then shows the reversals happening: the priest's sons sink, the lent child rises, the barren woman becomes a mother of six.
Read as a contrast of sons

The chapter cuts back and forth between Eli's sons and Samuel (2:11, 2:17–18, 2:21, 2:25–26). The sons of the priest despise the LORD; the boy from Ramah serves him. The reader learns early that birth and office do not guarantee faithfulness.

views.H: Traditional readers take the song as Hannah's own, a prophetic poem that foresees Israel's king. They read the oracle against Eli as fulfilled step by step: the deaths at Aphek (4:11), the massacre at Nob (22:18–19), and Solomon's removal of Abiathar in favor of Zadok (1 Kings 2:27, 35).
views.C: Most critical scholars think the song was a royal psalm, written for a king and placed in Hannah's mouth because of its line about the barren woman. The oracle of 2:27–36 is often read as written after Solomon, to explain why Zadok's family replaced Eli's.
views.L: The chapter is carefully arranged so the reader sees Samuel growing whenever the sons sink. The narrator also plants a detail: Eli's weight and the "honor" (kaved) his sons are given above God (2:29–30), a theme that pays off at Eli's death (4:18).
views.J: Hannah's song is the prophetic reading (haftarah) for the first day of Rosh Hashanah. The Targum turns the song into a prophecy of Israel's history down to the messiah. The Talmud defends Eli's sons, saying their sin was delaying the women's offerings, not adultery (Bavli Shabbat 55b).
views.X: Mary's song in Luke 1:46–55 follows Hannah's closely: the proud brought down, the humble lifted, the hungry filled. Luke's line that Jesus grew in favor with God and people echoes 2:26. Christian readers have seen the "faithful priest" of 2:35 fulfilled finally in Christ (Hebrews 2:17).

deep.b: Both songs begin with joy in God and both praise a God who reverses fortunes. Mary speaks of the mighty brought down from their thrones and the humble lifted up; Hannah of the bows of warriors broken and the poor lifted from the dust. Both end with God's promise to his people, Hannah with the king and anointed one, Mary with the promise to Abraham. The closest verbal link is in Hannah's prayer: in the Greek of 1:11 she asks God to look on the lowliness of his servant, and Mary sings that he has looked on the lowliness of his servant (Luke 1:48), with the same verb and nouns. Hannah's lines about lifting the poor and seating them with nobles (2:7–8) return in Mary's rulers brought down and lowly lifted up (Luke 1:52).

Leviticus gives the priest the breast and the right thigh of a peace offering (Leviticus 7:31–34), and Deuteronomy the shoulder, cheeks and stomach (Deuteronomy 18:3). The fat belonged to God and had to be burned first (Leviticus 3:16). Eli's sons break every part of this: they take whatever the fork brings up, they take meat before the fat is offered, and they threaten force. The people know the rules better than the priests (2:16).

echoes: Exodus 15:1–18; Deuteronomy 32:39; Psalm 113:7–9; Luke 1:46–55; Luke 2:52; 1 Kings 2:26–27; 1 Kings 2:35; Hebrews 2:17

settings.to: the LORD; the text names no other hearers
settings.when: after she has given Samuel to serve at the sanctuary
settings.why: The song praises the God who turns things upside down. The strong fall and the weak are lifted. The childless woman bears seven, and the poor are raised from the garbage heap to sit with nobles. It ends with God giving power to "his king" and "his anointed one" (2:10), before Israel has any king. She sings it at Shiloh, so the worshipers there probably heard it. Placed here, it tells the reader what the whole book will show: God brings down Eli's house and Saul, and raises a shepherd boy. Mary's song in Luke 1:46–55 echoes it.
views: Traditional readers take the song as Hannah's, spoken by a prophet who foresaw the coming king. Jewish tradition counts her among the prophetesses (Bavli Megillah 14a).
A royal psalm placed in her mouth

Many critical scholars think it was a psalm sung for the king, later set here by the book's editor because of the line about the childless woman. On this view the editor wanted readers to hear the story of kings framed by praise of the God who humbles the proud.

settings.to: his sons Hophni and Phinehas, priests at Shiloh
settings.when: after reports reach him of what his sons do to all Israel with the offerings
settings.why: The Hebrew text also says they slept with the women who served at the sanctuary entrance, a line missing from the Dead Sea scroll and the Greek. Eli argues that a sin against another person can be settled before God, but a sin against the LORD leaves no one to plead for the sinner. The warning is right but weak, and too late. The narrator adds that the sons would not listen because the LORD meant to put them to death. Readers see a father who speaks but does not act, which is the charge brought against him in the next oracle.

settings.what: A man of God's oracle against Eli's house
settings.by: an unnamed man of God, speaking for the LORD
settings.to: Eli the priest at Shiloh
settings.when: while his sons are abusing the sacrifices
settings.why: The oracle reminds Eli that God chose his ancestor's family in Egypt for the priesthood. Then it takes back the promise that they would serve forever: "I will honor the ones who honor me." It predicts the death of both sons on one day (fulfilled in 4:11), the slaughter of the priests (22:18–19), and a "faithful priest" who will serve God's anointed king. Readers of Kings saw it fulfilled when Solomon sent Eli's descendant Abiathar away and Zadok's line took over (1 Kings 2:27, 35).
views: Traditional readers see a prophecy spoken in Eli's time and fulfilled step by step over more than a century.
Many critical scholars think the oracle was shaped later to explain why Zadok's family, and not Eli's, held the priesthood in Jerusalem.

traditions.q: God promises a faithful priest. Does the church have priests, or is Christ the only priest?
views: Christ is the one high priest, and he shares his priesthood in two ways: all the baptized share a common priesthood, and ordained priests share a ministerial priesthood that differs in kind and offers the Eucharist in Christ's person (Catechism 1544–1547).
Bishops and priests serve at the altar in the person of Christ, who is the true celebrant of every liturgy, while all the faithful together form a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9).

All baptized Christians are priests (Luther, To the Christian Nobility). God has set up the public office of preaching and giving the sacraments (Augsburg Confession 5 and 14), but its ministers do not offer Christ again as a sacrifice.
Christ is our only high priest, who offered himself once for all (Heidelberg Catechism 31; Hebrews 10:12–14). Reformed churches call their leaders ministers or pastors, not priests.
Anglicans are divided. The ordination services keep the word priest, which Anglo-Catholics read in a sacrificial sense, while evangelical Anglicans take it simply to mean elder (presbyter).
Every believer is a priest with direct access to God through Christ, and the church's offices are pastors and deacons (Baptist Faith and Message, article 6).

title: The LORD calls Samuel
sum: In a time when the LORD's word is rare, the boy Samuel sleeps in the temple at Shiloh near the ark. The LORD calls him by name three times, and three times Samuel runs to Eli. At last Eli understands and tells him to answer, "Speak, LORD. Your servant is listening" (3:1–10).

The LORD's message is the doom of Eli's house, because Eli knew his sons were cursing God and did not stop them (3:11–14). In the morning Eli makes Samuel tell him everything, and accepts it: "He is the LORD" (3:15–18). Samuel grows up, none of his words fail, and all Israel knows him as a prophet (3:19–21).
readings: Read as a call story
Like Moses, Isaiah and Jeremiah, Samuel is called by God and given a hard message. His call is unusual because he does not recognize the voice, and the old priest has to teach him how to answer.
Read as a handing over
The lamp has not gone out, but Eli's eyes are dim. In one night the word of God passes from the old priest's house to the boy who lies near the ark. The rest of the chapter confirms the change.

views.H: Traditional readers take the call as a real experience of a boy of perhaps twelve (Josephus says Samuel was twelve). They often stress that God came and "took his stand" (3:10), a real presence, not only a voice.
views.C: Critics note that the chapter repeats the doom of 2:27–36 and may be a second version of it. Many see the chapter as legitimizing Samuel as prophet, linking him with the line of prophets Deuteronomy expected (Deuteronomy 18:15–18).
views.L: The story uses repetition with growing tension: three calls, three runs, and a fourth time with a changed answer. The reader knows who is speaking before Samuel does. Eli's dim eyes and the unextinguished lamp frame the scene in light and darkness.
views.J: Jewish tradition counted Samuel among the greatest prophets, compared with Moses and Aaron (Psalm 99:6; Jeremiah 15:1). Medieval Jewish commentators noticed that in 3:10 Samuel says only "Speak," without the word "LORD" that Eli gave him, and explained that he was not yet sure who was calling.
views.X: Christian writers use the chapter as a pattern of listening to God, and "Speak, LORD, your servant is listening" became a common prayer. Augustine and others saw in the passing of the priesthood from Eli to a new line a sign of the change from the old priesthood to Christ (City of God 17.5).

deep.h: Was Samuel sleeping in the Holy Place?
deep.b: The verse says Samuel lay "in the LORD's temple, where the ark of God stood" (3:3). In the law only the high priest could enter the room where the ark stood, once a year (Leviticus 16:2). Jewish interpreters such as Rashi and Radak read the verse to mean Samuel slept in a nearby room of the temple court, with the ark further in. Some modern scholars think practice at Shiloh was looser than the later law. The Plain gives the words as they stand.

echoes: Exodus 3:4; Isaiah 6:8; Jeremiah 1:4–10; Deuteronomy 18:15–22; Psalm 99:6; Jeremiah 15:1; Acts 3:24

settings.what: The LORD's first word to Samuel
settings.to: the boy Samuel, lying in the temple at Shiloh near the ark
settings.when: at night, in a time when the LORD's word was rare
settings.why: Samuel's first message from God is a hard one. The judgment already spoken against Eli's house will now happen, because Eli knew what his sons did and did not stop them. The boy must tell it to the man who raised him. That he tells it all, holding nothing back (3:18), proves him a true prophet. Readers learn that God's word has come back to Israel, through a child and not through the priests.

title: The ark is taken
sum: Israel goes out to fight the Philistines and loses four thousand men near Ebenezer. The elders decide to bring the ark of the covenant from Shiloh, sure it will save them. When it arrives the camp roars, and the Philistines are terrified, but they fight harder and win. Thirty thousand Israelites fall, the ark is captured, and Hophni and Phinehas are killed (4:1–11).

A runner from Benjamin reaches Shiloh with dirt on his head. Old blind Eli, waiting by the road, hears that the ark is taken, falls backward and breaks his neck (4:12–18). His daughter-in-law goes into labor at the news and dies, naming her son Ichabod, "Where is the glory?", for the glory has gone into exile from Israel (4:19–22).
readings: Read as a warning about religion as magic

Israel treats the ark as a weapon that will force God to fight. The disaster teaches that God cannot be used. The same lesson is drawn later about the temple (Jeremiah 7:12–14), with Shiloh as the example.
Read as the end of an era
In one day the priestly house falls, the sanctuary loses its ark, and the judge of forty years dies. The way is cleared for Samuel and, after him, for kings.

views.H: Traditional readers place the battle around 1050 BC, near Aphek (Tel Aphek, at the source of the Yarkon) and Ebenezer (perhaps Izbet Sartah, just east). Excavations at Shiloh found a destruction in the eleventh century BC, which many connect with this defeat (Psalm 78:60; Jeremiah 7:12).
views.C: Since Leonhard Rost, many scholars have read the ark chapters as an older "ark narrative" in which Samuel never appears. Rost marked it as 4:1b–7:1 with 2 Samuel 6; Patrick Miller and J. J. M. Roberts argued that it began with the sins of Eli's sons in chapter 2 and ended at 7:1, without 2 Samuel 6. They see it as a theological story explaining how the God of Israel could lose his ark and still be supreme.
views.L: The chapter is full of irony: the Philistines know the exodus story better than Israel, the shout of victory comes before a defeat, and heavy old Eli falls when he hears the ark is "taken." The word "glory" (kavod) and "heavy" (kaved) come from the same root.
views.J: Jewish tradition identified the Benjaminite runner as Saul, who snatched the tablets of the law from Goliath (Midrash Samuel, cited by Rashi). The rabbis taught that Israel was defeated because they trusted in the ark rather than in God.
views.X: Christian readers have used the chapter to warn against trusting in religious objects or forms instead of God. The departure of glory has been compared with Ezekiel's vision of glory leaving the temple (Ezekiel 10) and with John's claim that God's glory now lives in Jesus (John 1:14).

deep.b: The ark was a gold-covered chest holding the tablets of the covenant, with two cherubim above (Exodus 25:10–22). It was God's footstool and the sign of his throne; the LORD "sits on the cherubim" (4:4). In the wilderness it led the army (Numbers 10:35), and at Jericho it circled the walls (Joshua 6). Israel's elders remember those victories, but forget that the ark was never a guarantee.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the weight that falls
deep.b: My own reading: chapter 4 is built so that the "heavy" things fall. Eli is "heavy" (kaved, 4:18) because, the man of God said, he honored his sons and fattened himself on the offerings (2:29). The "glory" (kavod) of Israel departs (4:21–22). In the next chapter the LORD's hand is "heavy" (kaved) on the Philistines (5:6, 5:11). I suggest that the narrator moves the weight from Eli's body to God's hand: the weight Eli took for himself falls on him, and the true weight, God's, falls on the enemy. Scholars such as Polzin have traced the kbd wordplay; the shape of a transfer of weight is my own reading.

echoes: Numbers 10:35–36; Numbers 14:39–45; Joshua 6; Psalm 78:56–64; Jeremiah 7:12–14; Jeremiah 26:6; Ezekiel 10:18–19

settings.what: The elders' plan to fetch the ark
settings.to: the army, in the camp near Ebenezer
settings.when: after the Philistines kill about four thousand Israelites at Aphek
settings.why: The elders ask why the LORD let them lose, then answer their own question by sending for the ark of the covenant from Shiloh, so that it will "rescue us." They treat the ark like a weapon that forces God to fight. The plan leads to a far worse defeat, the ark's capture and the death of Eli's sons. Readers learn that God's presence cannot be used as a charm.

settings.to: each other, in their camp at Aphek
settings.when: when they hear Israel's war cry as the ark enters Israel's camp
settings.why: The enemy speaks the truth Israel has forgotten: this God struck Egypt. Their fear is greater than Israel's faith, since Israel treats the ark like a lucky charm. Yet the Philistines win. The scene tells readers that God cannot be carried into battle and used. He will act on his own terms, as chapters 5 and 6 show.

settings.by: the wife of Phinehas, dying in childbirth
settings.to: the women attending her at Shiloh
settings.when: on the day the ark was taken and her husband and father-in-law died
settings.why: She names her son Ichabod, "no glory," and says twice that glory has "gone into exile" from Israel. The verb is the one used for Israel's later exile. If the book took its final shape in the exile, readers in Babylon would have heard their own loss in her cry. The next chapters show that the God who seemed defeated was not.

title: The ark among the Philistines
sum: The Philistines carry the captured ark to the temple of their god Dagon in Ashdod and set it beside him. The next morning Dagon lies face down before the ark. They set him up again; the following morning he has fallen again, and his head and hands lie broken on the threshold (5:1–5).

The LORD's hand is heavy on Ashdod, striking the people with swellings. The ark is sent to Gath, and the plague follows; then to Ekron, whose people cry out that it will kill them all. Panic spreads, and the Philistine rulers are asked to send the ark home (5:6–12).
readings: Read as a contest of gods
Like the plagues of Egypt, the chapter shows Israel's God defeating another people's god on his own ground. No Israelite fights; the ark alone humbles Dagon and his worshipers.
Read as dark comedy
The chapter is told with humor: the Philistines keep picking Dagon up, then keep passing the ark from town to town like a hot coal. The great captured trophy becomes a burden no one wants.

views.H: Ashdod, Gath and Ekron were real Philistine cities, and excavations at Ashdod and Ekron (Tel Miqne) show their wealth in this period. Traditional readers see a real plague, perhaps carried by rodents, as the means of God's judgment.
views.C: Critics note that Dagon was worshiped by Semitic peoples long before the Philistines came, which suggests the Philistines adopted local gods. Scholars read the chapter as a theological polemic showing the LORD's power even in defeat.
views.L: The wordplay on "heavy" continues: the LORD's hand is heavy on the Philistines (5:6, 5:11). The threshold where Dagon's hands lie becomes a place the priests will not step on "to this day," a mocking explanation of a Philistine custom.
views.J: The Masoretic reading tradition replaces the written word for "swellings" with a more polite one, and the Talmud lists this among the places where a coarse word is read aloud in a gentler form (Bavli Megillah 25b). Zephaniah 1:9 condemns those who "leap over the threshold," which the Targum connects with this Philistine custom.
views.X: Christian preachers have read Dagon's fall as a picture of idols falling before the true God, and of Christ's victory over the powers (Colossians 2:15). Paul's teaching that an idol is nothing (1 Corinthians 8:4) has often been read alongside this chapter.

deep.b: The Hebrew word written in the text, ophalim, means "swellings" or "mounds"; the scribes' reading tradition replaced it with techorim, a word thought to mean "hemorrhoids" or "tumors." Because mice appear in chapter 6 and the plague spreads from town to town, many modern readers think of bubonic plague, which causes swellings (buboes) in the groin and is spread by rat fleas. Others think of dysentery. The text does not settle it.

echoes: Exodus 12:12; Exodus 9:3; Isaiah 19:1; Isaiah 46:1–2; Zephaniah 1:9; Judges 16:23–30

settings.what: The Philistine towns pass the ark along
settings.by: the men of Ashdod, the Philistine rulers, and the people of Ekron
settings.to: each other, and the five Philistine rulers
settings.when: as plague breaks out in each town that receives the ark
settings.why: Ashdod says Israel's God has been harsh on them and on Dagon. The rulers send the ark to Gath, and when plague follows, Ekron screams to send it home. Each speech admits what the Philistines will not say outright: the LORD has beaten their god in his own temple. The story assured Israel's readers that the LORD was not defeated when his ark was taken.

title: The ark comes home
sum: After seven months the Philistines ask their priests and diviners what to do. They advise sending the ark back with a guilt offering: five gold swellings and five gold mice, one for each ruler. They warn against hardening their hearts as Pharaoh did (6:1–6). As a test, they hitch two nursing cows that have never been yoked to a new cart; if the cows leave their calves and go straight to Beth-shemesh, the LORD sent the plague (6:7–9).

The cows go straight up the road, lowing as they go. At Beth-shemesh the harvesters rejoice, and the Levites offer the cows as a burnt offering on a great stone (6:10–18). But the LORD strikes some of the men of Beth-shemesh for looking into the ark, and they send it on to Kiriath-jearim (6:19–21).
readings: Read as an exodus in reverse

The Philistines quote the Egyptian plagues and Pharaoh's hard heart. Like Egypt they are struck by plagues, they send away the LORD with gold, and the LORD goes out from them. The ark's return replays the exodus with God himself coming home.
Read as a lesson in holiness

Even Israel cannot treat the ark carelessly. Joy at Beth-shemesh turns to grief, and the question "Who is able to stand in front of the LORD, this holy God?" (6:20) prepares for David's own fear in 2 Samuel 6.

views.H: Traditional readers see the cows' behavior as a real sign from God, since nursing cows would naturally turn back to their calves. Beth-shemesh is the excavated site of Tel Beth-shemesh on Judah's border with Philistia.
views.C: Critics compare the guilt offering with ancient practices of sending away a plague by making images of it, known from Mesopotamia and Greece. They see the Philistine priests as voicing the narrator's theology about Israel's God.
views.L: The narrator lets the Philistines speak Israel's theology: they quote the exodus, they "give honor" to Israel's God, and they devise a test that only God can pass. The cows, "mooing as they walked," give the scene a touch of humor and pathos.
views.J: The Talmud discussed the number struck at Beth-shemesh (Bavli Sotah 35b) and taught that they were punished for treating the ark with irreverence, looking at it while they kept working. The Levites' handling of the ark was taken as the correct way.
views.X: Christian readers saw in the cows going straight ahead, leaving their calves, a picture of obedience that leaves everything to follow God. The holiness of the ark was compared with the holiness of Christ's presence (Hebrews 12:28–29).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the LORD's own exodus
deep.b: My own reading: chapters 4–6 tell a small exodus in which the LORD himself is the captive. He goes into a foreign land, strikes it with plagues, is sent out with gold (compare Exodus 12:35–36), and returns to his people by a road no one guides. The Philistine priests even make the comparison (6:6). I suggest the story answers the question exile would later raise: if God's own symbol could be captured, he was not defeated, but chose to go out and come back. Scholars such as Patrick Miller and J. J. M. Roberts have noted the exodus language; reading the whole ark story as God's own exodus is my own framing.

echoes: Exodus 7–12; Exodus 12:35–36; Numbers 4:5–20; Numbers 19:2; Deuteronomy 21:3; 2 Samuel 6:1–11; Psalm 24:3

settings.to: the Philistine rulers and people
settings.when: after seven months of plague while the ark was in their land
settings.why: The priests tell the Philistines to send the ark home with a guilt offering of gold swellings and mice, and to test whether the LORD really sent the plague. They warn against hardening their hearts as Pharaoh and Egypt did. Foreign priests read the exodus better than Israel did in chapter 4. The test with the nursing cows, who leave their calves and walk straight to Beth-shemesh, shows readers that the LORD alone brought the ark back.

title: Ebenezer: so far the LORD has helped
sum: The ark stays at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years while Israel mourns after the LORD. Samuel calls Israel to put away the Baals and Ashtoreths and serve the LORD alone, and they do (7:1–4). At Mizpah the people pour out water, fast and confess. The Philistines attack, and Samuel offers a lamb and cries out to the LORD (7:5–9).

The LORD thunders against the Philistines and throws them into panic, and Israel chases them down. Samuel sets up a stone and names it Ebenezer, "stone of help" (7:10–12). The Philistines are held back all Samuel's days, the towns are recovered, and Samuel judges Israel on a yearly circuit from his home at Ramah (7:13–17).
readings: Read as the ideal judge

Samuel does everything a judge in Judges does, but without a sword: he calls the people back to God, prays for them, offers sacrifice, and God wins the battle. The chapter shows what Israel will give up when it asks for a king.
Read as a reversal of chapter 4
The same enemy, the same place name, Ebenezer, and the opposite result. In chapter 4 Israel trusted the ark; in chapter 7 they repent and pray. The second Ebenezer undoes the first.

views.H: Traditional readers take the victory as a real turning point, though they note that the Philistines are still strong in chapters 9–14. Many explain "all Samuel's days" as meaning the Philistines did not invade during his active judgeship.
views.C: Many critics see the chapter as idealized, written by the Deuteronomistic editor to show the pattern of sin, repentance and rescue. They point out that the Philistines are still in control in 10:5 and 13:3, and that Saul's wars are needed to defeat them.
views.L: The chapter takes up the Judges cycle (sin, cry, rescue, rest) and gives it a perfect form. Literary readers note the thunder that echoes Hannah's song (2:10) and the stone that answers the defeat at Ebenezer in 4:1.
views.J: The water poured out at Mizpah was explained in the Targum as pouring out hearts in repentance "like water." The rabbis compared Samuel to Moses and Aaron because he prayed for his people (Psalm 99:6).
views.X: "Here I raise my Ebenezer" in the hymn "Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing" (Robert Robinson, 1758) made this verse familiar to generations of Protestants. Christian readers often take 7:12 as a model of remembering God's help.

deep.b: The water ceremony at Mizpah (7:6) is not described elsewhere in the Bible. David pours out water from Bethlehem's well before the LORD (2 Samuel 23:16), and at the Feast of Booths in later times water was poured on the altar (Mishnah Sukkah 4:9). At Mizpah it is tied to fasting and confession; it may picture repentance as hearts poured out (Lamentations 2:19), or a solemn oath.

echoes: Judges 2:11–19; Judges 10:6–16; Deuteronomy 6:13; Lamentations 2:19; 2 Samuel 23:16; Psalm 99:6; Jeremiah 15:1

settings.what: Samuel's call to return to the LORD
settings.to: the whole house of Israel, and then all Israel gathered at Mizpah
settings.when: after twenty years with the ark at Kiriath-jearim, while the Philistines ruled the land
settings.why: Samuel tells Israel that if they come back to the LORD with their whole heart, they must remove the foreign gods and the Ashtoreths. They must serve him alone, and he will rescue them. The people confess, "We have sinned against the LORD." The pattern is the one taught in Deuteronomy and Judges: turning back to God comes before rescue. Later readers in exile heard the same call (Deuteronomy 30:1–3).

title: Give us a king
sum: Samuel grows old and makes his sons judges, but they take bribes. The elders of Israel come to Ramah and demand a king "like all the nations" (8:1–5). Samuel is displeased and prays. The LORD tells him to do what they ask: they have rejected not Samuel but God himself, as they always have (8:6–9).

Samuel warns the people what a king will do: take their sons for his army, their daughters for his kitchens, their best land for his officials, a tenth of their harvest and flocks, and finally their freedom. When they cry out because of him, the LORD will not answer (8:10–18). The people insist, wanting a king to lead them in war, and the LORD tells Samuel to give them one (8:19–22).
readings: Read as a rejection of God
God himself says the request rejects him as king. The chapter belongs with Gideon's refusal of a crown and Hosea's later judgment that God gave Israel a king in anger.
Read as a warning about power

Samuel's speech is one of the sharpest descriptions of state power in ancient literature. Readers from the Puritans to modern political thinkers have used it to argue that rulers tend to take, and that people should be careful what they ask for.

views.H: Traditional readers see the request as historical: the Philistine threat and the failure of Samuel's sons forced the issue. Many note that Deuteronomy 17 allows a king, and say the sin lay in the motive: to be like the nations and to trust a human king instead of God.
views.C: Since Wellhausen, critics have separated pro-kingship and anti-kingship sources in chapters 8–12, assigning this chapter to the later anti-monarchic strand. Others, after Mendelsohn, argue that the king's practices fit Canaanite kingship before Israel's monarchy and need not be late.
views.L: The narrator gives God's verdict, Samuel's hurt and the people's stubbornness, and lets them clash. Samuel's speech uses the verb "take" again and again (8:11–17). The people's last words, "like all the nations," repeat their first request (8:5, 8:20).
views.J: The Talmud debated whether appointing a king was a commandment (Bavli Sanhedrin 20b). Maimonides counted it as one of the commandments to fulfill on entering the land, and explained God's anger as directed at the spirit of the request. Don Isaac Abravanel, in the fifteenth century, used the chapter to argue that monarchy itself was not God's ideal.
views.X: Christian thinkers have read the chapter as part of a debate on government. Some, like Calvin, saw kingship as allowed by God; others, like John Milton and some Puritans, used it against absolute monarchy. Many Christians read the longing for a king as finally fulfilled in Jesus, the king who serves instead of taking (Mark 10:42–45).

deep.b: Deuteronomy 17:14–20 allows Israel a king, but forbids him to gather many horses, many wives, or great wealth, and requires him to copy and read God's law all his life. Samuel's speech in 8:11–17 is its mirror: everything the law forbids, the king "like the nations" will do. Readers have long noted how closely Solomon matches Samuel's warning, with his chariots, his many wives and his forced labor (1 Kings 10–11).

The book does not only argue against kings. Judges ends with a refrain, "There was no king in Israel in those days. Everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes" (Judges 17:6; Judges 21:25), and its last chapters show what that meant: idolatry, rape, civil war. Read after Judges, Israel's request answers a real need. God had promised Abraham that kings would come from him (Genesis 17:6), and Jacob's blessing gave Judah the scepter (Genesis 49:10). Deuteronomy plans for a king (Deuteronomy 17:14–20), and Hannah's song ends with God's king and anointed one (2:10). In 9:16 God himself sends Saul because he has heard his people's cry.

Scholars read the mix of voices in chapters 8–12 in different ways. The old source theory set a pro-kingship source against an anti-kingship one. Redaction critics such as Timo Veijola trace layers of Deuteronomistic editing, and McCarter a "prophetic history" that accepted kings under prophets. Literary readers such as Robert Polzin and Lyle Eslinger, and commentators such as David Tsumura, read the chapters as one argument: kingship is allowed, but a king like the nations' kings, who does not listen to God's word, is a rejection of God.

echoes: Deuteronomy 17:14–20; Deuteronomy 16:19; Judges 8:22–23; Judges 9:7–15; 1 Kings 12:4; Hosea 8:4; Hosea 13:10–11; Mark 10:42–45

settings.what: The elders ask for a king
settings.to: Samuel, at Ramah
settings.when: when Samuel is old and his sons, judges at Beersheba, take bribes
settings.why: The elders point to a real problem: Samuel is old and his sons bend justice. But their answer is to ask for a king "to judge us, like all the nations." Israel was meant to be different from the nations. The request drives the rest of the book, and the cards that follow (8:7–9; 8:11–18) are God's and Samuel's replies.

settings.what: The LORD's answer about a king
settings.to: Samuel, who has prayed after the elders asked for a king
settings.when: at Ramah, when Samuel is old and his sons take bribes
settings.why: God tells Samuel the people have not rejected him but God himself, as they have done since Egypt. Yet God tells him to listen to them and give them a king, with a clear warning. This sets up the book's double view of kingship: the request is a sin, and God still grants it and works through it.

settings.what: Samuel's warning about the ways of the king
settings.to: the elders of Israel and the people asking him for a king, at Ramah
settings.when: after they ask for a king "like all the nations"
settings.why: Samuel lists what a king will take. He will take sons for his chariots and fields, daughters for his kitchens, and the best land for his servants. He will take a tenth of the harvest and flocks, and finally their freedom. The key verb is "take." The warning is meant to make the people count the cost before they choose. It ends with a threat: when they cry out because of their king, the LORD will not answer. Readers who lived under Solomon's forced labor (1 Kings 5:13; 1 Kings 12:4) knew how true it was.
views: A warning drawn from real kings of the time
Isaac Mendelsohn showed that texts from Ugarit describe Canaanite kings taking land, labor and a tenth of produce in just this way. So the speech fits kingship in Samuel's own age.
Many critical scholars think the speech was shaped by bitter experience of Solomon and later kings, and belongs to the anti-monarchy strand of the book or to the Deuteronomistic editor.
Many readers compare it with Deuteronomy 17:14–20, which allows a king but forbids him to pile up horses, wives and gold.

settings.what: The people insist on a king
settings.to: Samuel, at Ramah
settings.when: after Samuel's warning about the ways of the king
settings.why: The people refuse to listen. They want a king to judge them, march out at their head and fight their wars, so that they will be like all the nations. They want security in war, which the Philistine threat made urgent. Readers notice that the LORD had fought for them at Mizpah (7:10), so the request also shows a loss of trust.

title: Lost donkeys and a hidden king
sum: Kish, a wealthy Benjaminite, sends his tall, handsome son Saul with a servant to find some lost donkeys. After days of searching they reach the land of Zuph, and the servant suggests asking a man of God in the town, paying him with a quarter shekel of silver (9:1–10). Girls at the well tell them the seer has come for a sacrifice at the high place (9:11–14).

The day before, the LORD told Samuel that he would send a Benjaminite to be ruler over Israel and rescue them from the Philistines. When Saul appears, the LORD says, "This is the man" (9:15–17). Samuel tells Saul the donkeys are found, hints at his future, and seats him at the head of thirty guests with the choice portion. The next morning, at the edge of town, Samuel stops him to give him the word of God (9:18–27).
readings: Read as a folk tale

A young man looking for lost animals finds a kingdom. The story has the shape of a folk tale: the helpful servant, the girls at the well, the mysterious seer who knows everything. Its charm is part of its meaning: God chooses through ordinary errands.
Read as God answering the people

Chapter 8 ended with God telling Samuel to give the people a king. Chapter 9 shows God choosing the man himself and giving him a task: rescue from the Philistines. The king the people asked for is also the ruler God gives.

views.H: Traditional readers identify the unnamed town as Ramah, Samuel's home, and trace Saul's route through the hill country of Ephraim and Benjamin. They see Saul's anointing as God's real choice of a good man who later failed.
views.C: Many critics see an old folk tale about a nameless seer, later linked to Samuel, and note that this account is friendlier to kingship than chapter 8. God's words in 9:16 present kingship as his own answer to Israel's cry.
views.L: The narrator builds dramatic irony: the reader knows from 9:15–16 what Saul does not. Saul's questions to the girls and to Samuel himself (9:18) are comic, and Samuel's hints (9:20) are deliberately mysterious.
views.J: In the Talmud (Bavli Berakhot 48b) Rabbi Natan cites 9:13, "it's his job to bless the sacrifice," as a source for saying a blessing over a meal. Rabbinic tradition praised Saul's modesty and his concern for his father (9:5), and said the girls talked at length so they could look at his beauty.
views.X: Christian readers have contrasted Saul, chosen for his height and looks, with David, chosen for his heart (16:7). Paul mentions Saul's forty years as king and his tribe of Benjamin, which was also Paul's own (Acts 13:21; Philippians 3:5).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the man who is always being looked for
deep.b: My own reading: Saul's story begins with a search for something lost, and Saul keeps being the one searched for. The donkeys are lost and found (9:3, 9:20), but at Mizpah Saul himself is the lost one, "he could not be found" (10:21), and must be dug out from the baggage. Later Saul will search for David in the wilderness and not find him (23:14; 26:20). I suggest the narrator uses "seeking" and "finding" to show a king who is never quite where he should be. Scholars have noted the donkey motif; this thread through the whole story is my own reading.

echoes: Genesis 24:11–15; Exodus 2:15–17; Exodus 3:7–9; Judges 6:15; Judges 13:2; 1 Chronicles 9:35–39; Acts 13:21

settings.what: The LORD tells Samuel of Saul
settings.to: Samuel, privately
settings.when: the day before Saul arrives looking for his father's donkeys
settings.why: God says he is sending a man from Benjamin whom Samuel is to anoint as "ruler" (Hebrew nagid). The man will rescue Israel from the Philistines, "for I have seen my people; their cry has come to me." The words echo the call of Moses (Exodus 3:7–9). After chapter 8, readers learn that the king is not only the people's demand. God also gives him, as an answer to their cry.

title: Anointed, changed, chosen by lot
sum: Samuel pours oil on Saul's head and anoints him ruler over the LORD's people. He gives three signs: men at Rachel's tomb will say the donkeys are found, travelers at the oak of Tabor will give him bread, and at Gibeah he will meet a band of prophets, and the Spirit of the LORD will sweep down on him. He is told to wait for Samuel at Gilgal seven days (10:1–8). All the signs come true; God gives Saul another heart, and he prophesies, giving rise to the saying "Is Saul among the prophets too?" (10:9–13). Saul tells his uncle nothing about the kingship (10:14–16).

Samuel gathers Israel at Mizpah, rebukes them for rejecting God, and has the tribes come forward. The lot falls on Benjamin, then on Saul, who is found hiding among the baggage. Taller than everyone, he is acclaimed: "Long live the king!" Samuel writes the rules of the kingdom in a scroll. Some men despise Saul, and Nahash the Ammonite is crushing the tribes beyond the Jordan (10:17–27).
readings: Read as three steps to kingship
Saul is first anointed in secret, then chosen publicly by lot, and in chapter 11 proved in battle and confirmed. Many readers see an ancient pattern: designation, demonstration, confirmation.
Read as a gift and a warning

Saul is given everything: anointing, signs, the Spirit, a new heart, the people's shout. But he is also given a command to wait (10:8), and his hiding shows a man not sure of himself. The chapter plants the seeds of his later failure.

views.H: Traditional readers take the anointing, the signs and the lot as real events, with the lot guided by God (Proverbs 16:33). They see Saul's hiding as genuine modesty and the "rules of the kingdom" as a real written charter.
views.C: Many critics see two accounts of Saul's choice, a secret anointing (9:1–10:16) friendly to kingship and a public lot (10:17–27) framed by Samuel's anti-monarchic speech. Many accept the 4QSam-a Nahash paragraph at 10:27 as original text.
views.L: The chapter plays with sight and hiding: the tallest man in Israel hides, the man who can see the future gives signs, and Saul's uncle cannot get a straight answer. The prophets' proverb, and the question "who is their father?", leave the reader unsure what to think of Saul.
views.J: The Talmud praised Saul's modesty, seen in his silence about the kingdom in 10:16 (Bavli Megillah 13b), and read 13:1 to mean that Saul was like a one-year-old, free of sin, when he began to reign (Bavli Yoma 22b). The "rules of the kingdom" were identified with the law of the king in Deuteronomy 17.
views.X: The anointing of Saul is a key text for the meaning of "messiah," the anointed one. Christian readers note that the Spirit comes on Saul for a task and can leave him (16:14), and contrast it with the Spirit resting on Jesus (Isaiah 11:2; Luke 4:18).

deep.b: Samuel's three signs move Saul from his lost errand to his new calling. The first ends the donkey search; the second, men going up to God at Bethel, gives the future king bread as a kind of gift; the third, the band of prophets, brings the Spirit. Each sign comes true "that day" (10:9), confirming that Samuel speaks for God. The command to wait seven days at Gilgal (10:8) is not fulfilled until 13:8, where it becomes Saul's undoing.

deep.h: Lots and the will of God
deep.b: Israel used lots to divide land (Joshua 18:10), to find the guilty (Joshua 7:14–18; 14:41–42) and to choose leaders, as here and later in the choice of Matthias (Acts 1:26). The Urim and Thummim were probably a kind of sacred lot (14:41). Proverbs 16:33 says the lot is cast into the lap, but every decision is from the LORD. The same method that found Achan finds Saul.

echoes: Genesis 35:16–20; Exodus 29:7; Numbers 11:25–29; Joshua 7:14–18; Judges 6:34; Judges 14:6; Deuteronomy 17:14–20; Proverbs 16:33; Acts 1:26

settings.what: Samuel anoints Saul and gives him signs
settings.to: Saul, alone at the far end of the town where they met (the text does not name it)
settings.when: at dawn, after the young man is sent on ahead
settings.why: Samuel anoints Saul in secret. He gives him three signs to prove the anointing is from God: men with news of the donkeys, three pilgrims with bread, and a band of prophets. When the Spirit comes, Saul will be "turned into another man." Samuel also tells him to wait seven days at Gilgal. That last order sets the test Saul fails in 13:8–14.

settings.by: people who had known Saul before
settings.to: each other, at Gibeah
settings.when: when they see Saul prophesying with a band of prophets
settings.why: The question became a saying. It expresses surprise that the son of Kish, a farmer's son, should be found among the prophets. Someone asks, "And who is their father?", which may mean that prophets have no famous family, so anyone can join them. The saying comes back in 19:24 in a darker setting, when Saul lies stripped before Samuel.

settings.to: the Israelites gathered before the LORD at Mizpah, tribe by tribe
settings.when: before the king is chosen by lot
settings.why: Samuel reminds them that the LORD brought them out of Egypt and rescued them, and says that by asking for a king they have rejected their God. Then he lets the lot choose the king. The speech makes sure that Israel never forgets the cost, even as it receives what it asked for.

settings.to: all the people, and the new king Saul, at Mizpah
settings.when: after Saul is chosen and acclaimed
settings.why: Samuel tells the people the rules of the kingship, writes them in a scroll and places it before the LORD. The text does not give them. They bound both king and people, and they set the king under God and his prophet, not over them. Many readers compare the law of the king in Deuteronomy 17:14–20, which tells the king to keep a copy of the law and read it all his life.
views: Many scholars, Baruch Halpern among them, see a real constitution here: an agreement setting the king's duties and limits.
Others think the editor wants readers to think of Deuteronomy 17:14–20, so that Saul's later failures are judged by it.

title: Saul rescues Jabesh
sum: Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead and offers a treaty only if every man's right eye is put out. The elders ask for seven days to seek help (11:1–3). When the news reaches Gibeah, Saul is coming in from the field behind his oxen. The Spirit of God sweeps down on him; he cuts up his oxen and sends the pieces through Israel, threatening the same to anyone who will not follow. Israel turns out as one man (11:4–8).

Saul tells Jabesh that help will come by noon tomorrow. He attacks in three companies at dawn and scatters the Ammonites (11:9–11). The people want to kill those who had despised Saul, but Saul refuses: today the LORD has rescued Israel. Samuel leads the people to Gilgal, where Saul is made king before the LORD with sacrifices and great joy (11:12–15).
readings: Read as Saul's finest hour
Saul acts like the best of the judges: moved by the Spirit, quick, bold and merciful. The chapter shows the promise of Saul's kingship before it goes wrong.
Read as Judges undone
The story is full of echoes of Judges 19–21: Gibeah, Jabesh-gilead, a body cut in pieces and sent through Israel, the tribes gathering as one man. What began as Israel's worst crime ends as a rescue.

views.H: Traditional readers see a real campaign across the Jordan, with Bezek opposite Jabesh. They often note that Nahash of Ammon was later friendly to David (2 Samuel 10:2), perhaps because David was Saul's enemy.
views.C: Many critics regard this chapter as the oldest and most historical account of how Saul became king, a deliverer like the judges acclaimed after victory. They see "renew the kingdom" (11:14) as an editor's link to 10:17–27.
views.L: The chapter's structure moves from humiliation to triumph within a week. The men of Jabesh speak with a double meaning (11:10). Saul's mercy to his critics (11:13) balances the threat he sends with the oxen (11:7).
views.J: Jewish commentators have admired Saul for refusing revenge on the day of victory. Josephus expands the chapter, explaining the right-eye threat and describing Nahash's earlier campaign (Antiquities 6.68–80), which agrees with the 4QSam-a paragraph at 10:27.
views.X: Christian readers have seen Saul's Spirit-led rescue as an example of God's power working through a willing person, and his mercy as a sign of the kingship God intended. The contrast with his later decline has made him a classic example of a good start that ends badly.

deep.b: The Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a contains a paragraph before 11:1, now printed in 10:27 of the Plain, that tells of Nahash's earlier campaign. Josephus, retelling Samuel around AD 94, includes the same information: Nahash had been putting out the right eyes of the Israelites across the Jordan, and a month later besieged Jabesh. This agreement shows that Josephus used a Hebrew or Greek text of Samuel that had the paragraph, and that it was not invented by the Qumran scribe.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Jabesh frames Saul's reign
deep.b: My own reading: Saul's public reign begins and ends with Jabesh-gilead. His first act as king is to save the town (11:1–11); after his death the men of Jabesh walk all night to rescue his body from Beth-shan and give it burial (31:11–13). I suggest the narrator intends this frame as a judgment on Saul's life: whatever else he lost, the people he rescued did not forget him. David himself praises Jabesh for its loyalty (2 Samuel 2:5–6). Commentators note the link; reading it as the deliberate frame of the whole reign is my own suggestion.

echoes: Judges 19:29–30; Judges 20:1; Judges 21:8–14; Judges 7:16; Judges 6:11; 31:11–13; 2 Samuel 2:4–7; 2 Samuel 10:1–2

settings.to: all the territory of Israel, through messengers carrying pieces of oxen
settings.when: after Nahash the Ammonite threatens to put out the right eyes of Jabesh-gilead
settings.why: Saul cuts up his oxen and warns that whoever does not follow him and Samuel will see his oxen treated the same way. It is a curse that binds every tribe to come. The act recalls the Levite who cut up his concubine to summon the tribes (Judges 19:29), and the rescue of the same town of Jabesh. The new king proves himself like the old judges, and wins the people's loyalty.

settings.to: Samuel, then the people
settings.when: after the rescue of Jabesh-gilead
settings.why: The people want to kill the men who mocked Saul (10:27). Saul refuses: no one will die "today the LORD has won a rescue in Israel." The new king gives the credit to God and unites the people rather than taking revenge. It is Saul at his best, and readers will compare him with what follows.
